item.title: Ascension Island: How a planting project created a lush cloud forest
item.description: In the middle of nowhere, a small island emerges in the Atlantic Ocean. This unique territory completely changed in the 19th century thanks to the efforts of two British scientists: Charles Darwin and Joseph Dalton Hooker, researchers who stopped at the British naval base and documented the island during their expeditions. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Could the dodo return? US firm maps 95% of its genome and identifies gene-editing targets
item.description: Colossal Biosciences aims to resurrect the extinct dodo bird using cutting-edge gene-editing technologies. By leveraging their sophisticated AI platform, GenoMorph, the company has pinpointed essential genetic traits. With 95% of the dodo genome analysis complete, their ambitious project is on track, though a specific timeline for the living dodo remains undisclosed. This groundbreaking venture is part of a larger initiative to counteract the effects of human-induced species extinction. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: Archaeologists find 19 injuries in 12 people buried in Iron and Viking Age Scandinavia
item.description: Archaeologists found evidence of traumatic injuries in 12 individuals from Iron and Viking Age Scandinavia. These injuries were discovered in domestic spaces like houses, pits, and wells across various sites. Examination of the remains revealed sharp-force and blunt-force injuries indicating potential violence in their lives. Researchers proposed that social conditions may have contributed to the unusual burial practices observed. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: Montana rancher’s rare Nanotyrannus fossil goes on display ahead of $9M auction
item.description: A rare find in the form of a nearly 70 percent complete Nanotyrannus skeleton, affectionately named Jodi, has been unearthed by rancher Jodi Pierson in Montana and is set to go under the hammer at Sotheby’s in New York on October 27. This well-preserved specimen is anticipated to garner between $6 million and $9 million, creating a buzz among paleontologists and collectors alike due to its invaluable significance. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: Tech Aids Lost Birdsong Recovery: Synthetic calls help sparrows relearn old songs; scientists weigh AI’s role
item.description: A groundbreaking approach has emerged, leveraging computer-generated recordings to rejuvenate the bird songs that nature has lost. Researchers successfully reintroduced the unique call of the rufous-collared sparrow back into its habitat in Argentina. This innovative conservation strategy seeks to bolster endangered species by preserving their vocal heritage and fostering communication skills, as demonstrated by positive outcomes in captive breeding for species such as the regent honeyeater. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: Ozempic and Wegovy linked to rare risk of sudden vision loss
item.description: Popular diabetes and weight loss drugs such as Ozempic and Wegovy have been linked to a slightly increased risk of a rare condition that can cause sudden, potentially permanent vision loss. Although the risk remains very low, Rutgers researchers say the findings warrant attention as millions of people turn to GLP-1 medications. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Fires Arrive in the Amazon Rainforest
item.description: During El Niño, a cascade of fires across the tropics begins in equatorial Asia and continues in the central and eastern Amazon. Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Consumers need clearer answers before they can trust precision fermentation, new report finds
item.description: Consumers may not fully understand precision fermentation yet, but many are curious enough to taste the results. New qualitative research from the EIT Food Consumer Observatory, published ahead of World Food Day on Oct. 16, suggests that this curiosity creates an important opportunity for food innovation, provided companies can answer consumers' questions clearly and deliver on the first bite. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Now you see them: Researchers uncover patterns in vessels that vanish at sea
item.description: Across the waters of West Africa, commercial fishing vessels vanish along international boundary lines. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists alarmed as super El Niño collides with 'strange uptick' in Galapagos iguana trafficking
item.description: The only lizard in the world that can live and forage at sea may now be in a fight for survival. International scientists warn black-market trafficking of Galapagos marine iguanas is peaking just as the super El Niño decimates their natural food source. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Climate adaptation's delivery gap: Turning national plans into action
item.description: By 2025, 143 of 154 developing countries had a National Adaptation Plan process in place, yet implementation has not kept pace. Many countries still lack the institutional capacity, project preparation and finance needed to turn their priorities into strategies, bankable projects and results on the ground. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Social service agencies need safeguards when using AI
item.description: Artificial intelligence is increasingly being used by social service agencies to handle cases involving child abuse, intimate partner violence and elder abuse. But a University of Iowa researcher and former social worker says the agencies need to establish safeguards to ensure that AI technology does not lead to bias against vulnerable or disadvantaged populations. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Can AI feel safer than human advice for consumers who face discrimination?
item.description: What should you cook for dinner on a budget of 20 euros when you have a guest with a gluten intolerance? A shopper might ask a shop assistant for advice or consult, for example, Hopla, the AI-powered shopping assistant launched by French supermarket chain Carrefour. Behind this everyday choice lies a broader question: when faced with a recommendation, who do we trust more? A human being or an AI? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A 47-year study reveals the age when your body starts losing strength
item.description: A 47-year study has uncovered a surprising turning point in physical aging: fitness and strength begin declining around age 35, even among people who exercise regularly. Researchers found that this decline accelerates as people get older, but starting to exercise in adulthood can still improve physical performance. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Fair climate transitions need more than financial support, evidence review suggests
item.description: The transition to a low-carbon economy will not affect all people and places equally. Although its overall benefits may outweigh its costs, workers may lose jobs, households may face higher prices and communities dependent on carbon-intensive industries may experience lasting economic and social disruption. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Green, pink and purple: Astronomers reveal the surprising true colors of white dwarf stars
item.description: University of Warwick astronomers have shown that white dwarf stars can glow in a range of colors, including the first star ever found that would appear green to the human eye. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Researchers in exile thrive in new academic settings when they contribute knowledge, not just receive aid
item.description: Publishing scientific articles requires more than knowledge of academic writing conventions; it also depends on access to networks that support the research and publication process. Academic networks provide opportunities to exchange knowledge, receive feedback and develop collaborations that can strengthen both research and careers. For researchers in vulnerable situations, such connections can be crucial. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA develops batteries to power humanity's return to moon
item.description: If you've ever had your car start sluggishly, or not at all, on a particularly frigid winter morning, you know standard batteries do not like extreme cold. That's why NASA researchers are working to develop a battery that could function in the brutal cold of the moon's south pole, where nighttime temperatures plunge to minus 328 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 200 degrees Celsius). Publicado también por: NASA. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists reveal 93% of Australia's Indigenous population was lost in just 73 years
item.description: A groundbreaking study suggests that 2.22 million Indigenous Australians lived on the continent before European colonization, far more than previously believed. Researchers estimate that 93% of this population was lost within 73 years, revealing a demographic catastrophe on a scale that dramatically changes our understanding of Australian history. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

I was watching this on a livestream (not SpaceX official stream) and the commenters spotted it. Then looking at the replays they were pretty much convinced it was the ISS. Which makes sense because the spacecraft launched is headed for the ISS and the timing of the launch must be such that it matches the ISS orbital plane alignment.

item.title: Uganda's sugarcane boom leaves families hungry: What needs to change
item.description: Busoga, in eastern Uganda, is a low, fertile plateau surrounded on three sides by Lake Victoria, the Nile River and Lake Kyoga. Most of its 4.3 million people farm small, rain-fed plots. Yet hunger is common: in the 2024 census, about a third of Busoga households reported going whole days without food. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Fine particles from aircraft exhaust become more harmful over time, lab tests suggest
item.description: Fine particulate matter consists of tiny particles with diameters in the nanometer range. They are produced, for example, by fuel combustion, remain suspended in the air and can penetrate deep into the respiratory tract. There, they can trigger oxidative stress, a process that promotes inflammation and, over the long term, can lead to serious health problems such as respiratory or cardiovascular diseases. Scientists call this harmful property the particles' oxidative potential. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New chip-scale gyroscope measures rotation with unprecedented sensitivity
item.description: Researchers have developed a chip-scale optical ring-laser gyroscope that can measure rotation as slow as 37 degrees per hour. This record sensitivity, approaching Earth's rotation rate of 15 degrees per hour, could eventually be useful for precision navigation and orientation systems, particularly where GPS is unavailable. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A trip to Mars could come at a heartbreaking cost
item.description: When astronauts first travel to Mars or anywhere else in deep space, they will have to contend with two problems that our planet protects us from on its surface—radiation and weightlessness. Scientists already know both can have a profound impact on the human body, but the extent of that impact and how long it can last remain a mystery. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A forgotten fossil reveals a fearsome dinosaur with giant claws
item.description: A 120-million-year-old fossil forgotten in a museum for nearly a century has revealed a terrifying new dinosaur that may have been more dangerous to humans than a T. rex. The tiger-sized predator also provides the first evidence of megaraptorans in Europe, helping explain how these mysterious dinosaurs eventually became gigantic hunters. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Urbanization takes a bigger toll on bird diversity in the tropics than it does at other latitudes, study finds
item.description: Researchers at McGill University have found that urbanization is weakening one of Earth's most enduring ecological patterns: the tendency for biodiversity to increase toward the tropics, a pattern known as the latitudinal diversity gradient. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: When parents don't see eye to eye: Are differences in parenting styles a bad thing?
item.description: Sometimes it can be hard for parents to agree on how to raise children. One parent might insist their child's homework has to be finished before they're allowed to use devices. The other may think a bit of screen time before studying is perfectly reasonable. Rules and consequences might be the preferred strategy of one parent, while the other favors a more flexible approach. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Rocket Lab’s stock slides as the company pushes back Neutron’s first launch
item.description: Neutron, a medium-lift rocket meant to rival SpaceX’s Falcon 9, will no longer launch this year. Fuente: MarketWatch.
item.dc:creator: William Gavin

item.title: Waste plastics become molecular sponges that capture water from air
item.description: Discarded plastic packaging materials, old CDs and even LEGO bricks can be transformed into materials that capture significant amounts of moisture from the air. Materials chemists Anastasiia Naryshkina, Paul Schweng and Robert Woodward at the University of Vienna have converted several types of plastic waste into water-attracting polymer networks that take up water even in dry climates and release it again under moderate heating, for example, using sunlight. The study, published in Chem Circularity, offers a route to give plastic waste a second life as an adsorbent for atmospheric water… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Spawning coral release quintillions of eggs each year, new calculations suggest
item.description: Most kinds of coral spawn once a year. In an enormous multiday event synchronized to specific phases of the moon, they release vast slicks of eggs and sperm into the ocean to be mixed together by the drifting currents. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Cancer is rising in younger adults, and scientists can't fully explain why
item.description: A major study found that several cancers are rising faster among younger adults in England, even as smoking, diet, and other established risk factors have generally improved. Excess weight explains only part of the increase, leaving scientists searching for other possible causes, including changes in the gut microbiome and early-life exposures. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Genome publishing overhaul targets 200 reports per month, up from 30
item.description: The Wellcome Sanger Institute's Tree of Life program plans to accelerate publication of genome notes from approximately 30 per month to 200, expanding access to research that is supporting advances in agriculture, conservation and medicine. This increase will be facilitated by a new specialized workflow developed by F1000 and the Wellcome Sanger Institute for Wellcome Open Research. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A single carbon atom stitches flat molecules into 3D structures
item.description: Flat is fine for a sheet of paper, but many of the most useful molecules need depth. Now, researchers from Japan have found a way to give them that depth using nothing more than a single carbon atom. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How E. coli eavesdrops on the metabolic activity of other gut bacteria
item.description: The gut microbiome is teeming with hundreds of bacterial species and trillions of bacteria. These microorganisms influence many aspects of health, including digestion, and assist with numerous functions in the body. Gut bacteria compete for the limited nutrients available in their environment, while also interacting with each other in ways that can influence the stability of the microbial community. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: From 'A Little Princess' to 'Black Panther,' how Hollywood films have reimagined the South Asian epic 'Ramayana'
item.description: American audiences will be able to watch an English-dubbed version of "Ramayana," a Hindi film based on a South Asian epic tradition, in theaters in November 2026. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How detection dogs are helping protect one of Australia's most imperiled lizards
item.description: Many of the Australian animals most at risk of extinction are extremely tough to track down. That's because they live in small pockets of disappearing nature, such as rare grasslands or ancient forests, in worryingly low numbers. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists identify avian cholera as major cause of penguin deaths in Antarctica
item.description: Thousands of Adélie penguins found dead in Antarctica in 2024 were primarily victims of avian cholera, not high pathogenicity avian influenza (H5N1) as researchers initially suspected, according to a study published today in Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences. The findings highlight an underrecognized threat to Antarctic wildlife and the importance of comprehensive disease investigations, particularly as H5N1 continues to raise concerns for seabird and marine mammal populations. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Engineered enzyme could improve detection of HIV and other viruses
item.description: Scientists have long used a powerful gene-editing tool called CRISPR to make precise changes to DNA. But a different version of the technology, known as Cas13a, targets RNA, the genetic material found in viruses such as HIV. Now, researchers at Rice University have developed an improved version of Cas13a that could make it easier to detect HIV and other RNA viruses in blood and environmental samples. The study was published in Cell Chemical Biology. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Firms facing tariff shocks choose collaboration over conquest
item.description: New research has charted the way U.S. businesses adapted to market shocks caused by reductions in import tariffs and increased foreign competition, with greater innovation emerging as a longer-term benefit. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI-assisted math advance highlights gap between finding answers and judging their significance
item.description: AI models are good at finding answers to mathematical puzzles but are not as good at research judgment, according to theoretical computer scientists. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Things are finally looking up for NASA's first missions to Venus in a generation
item.description: "This is great news for us. We're staffing up. We're accelerating." Fuente: Ars Technica.
item.dc:creator: Stephen Clark

item.title: International business is influenced by local political climate, study finds
item.description: A new study co-authored by Tang Yinuo, a tenured associate professor at Peking University HSBC Business School (PHBS), reveals that conservative communities in the U.S. are more likely to resist mergers and acquisitions (M&As) by Chinese companies due to perceived threats and uncertainties. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Mollusk family trees play a key role in shaping microbiomes, researchers find
item.description: A mollusk's microbial community has more to do with its family tree than its address. In other words, the composition of a mollusk's microbiome depends less on the environment in which it lives and more on what species it belongs to, say University of Michigan researchers. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Examining fraud prevention in federal relief programs
item.description: SUNY Polytechnic Institute (SUNY Poly) assistant professor of accounting Dr. Katie Matt, in collaboration with Daniel Hebert of Syracuse University, recently published research examining the widespread fraud associated with the federal Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) during the COVID-19 pandemic. Their article, "Governance and Fraud Prevention in Federal Relief Programs: Insights from the Paycheck Protection Program," was published in the Journal of Accounting, Ethics & Public Policy in September 2026. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New framework links magnetic phase boundaries to string-like defects in spin ice
item.description: A research team led by Haruki Watanabe, a professor in the Department of Physics and the Jockey Club Institute for Advanced Study (IAS) at The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST), in collaboration with professor Yukitoshi Motome and graduate student Sena Watanabe from the University of Tokyo, has developed a unified theory that predicts when two states of matter are genuinely distinct and when they are actually the same. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: In 1930, a Pittsburgh plumber built an aluminium observatory that helped him meet Einstein
item.description: Established in 1930 by Leo Scanlon, the Valley View Observatory in Pittsburgh quickly gained traction among amateur astronomers, primarily due to its cost-effective construction and unique aluminium dome. Scanlon's fresh approach drew attention from enthusiasts nationwide, leading to a memorable encounter with Albert Einstein in 1934, who appreciated the spirit of amateur science. To honor its significant role in astronomy, asteroid 8131 was named 'Scanlon', recognizing the observatory's legacy. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: NASA to Host News Conference Previewing US Spacewalks 100, 101
item.description: NASA will preview two upcoming spacewalks to complete solar array installation and power augmentation of the International Space Station during a news conference at 2 p.m. EDT, Tuesday, Oct. 20, from NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston. NASA will stream the event through a variety of platforms. Learn where to watch online: https://www.nasa.gov/live NASA participants […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Jessica Taveau

item.title: Job loss and AI-exposed jobs: Q&A with sociology professor
item.description: Jennie Brand, a UCLA professor of sociology with an appointment in statistics and data science, is an expert on the socioeconomic effects of job loss, including the long-term economic, psychological, physiological and intergenerational effects. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Learning reshapes inhibitory synapses differently within the same nerve cell, study suggests
item.description: Our brain must be able to learn new things without losing previously stored information or the stability of its networks. Researchers at the Leibniz Institute for Neurobiology (LIN) in Magdeburg, together with partners in Bielefeld and Zurich, have investigated how this balance is achieved. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Rare particle decays hint at deviations from Standard Model predictions
item.description: Studying rare processes is part and parcel of particle physics, providing stringent tests of the Standard Model. At the recent International Conference on High Energy Physics (ICHEP), the CMS and LHCb collaborations presented their latest research into one such process: the transformation of a beauty quark into a strange quark, a muon and the oppositely charged antimuon (b→sμ⁺μ⁻). Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Sheep grazing in solar fields offers farmers economic, ecological gains
item.description: Two new research papers shed light on the growing practice of grazing sheep in fields with solar arrays. One demonstrates that, in the right numbers, sheep grazing increases populations of beneficial insects like bees and lady beetles compared to mowing around solar panels. The other research describes a decision-making support tool to help farmers profitably grow their solar grazing herds. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Superheavy-element compound reveals weaker-than-expected bond due to relativistic effects
item.description: An international collaboration led by a research group from GSI/FAIR in Darmstadt, Germany, has achieved the first measurement of the chemical stability of a superheavy element compound. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Employees look to leaders as study finds gap between workplace promises and employee experience
item.description: A survey of UK employees has revealed that more than half experience a mismatch between what their employer says and what they do in practice, with many looking to leadership behavior when judging an organization's true values. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Earth's mantle was 'breathing' oxygen a billion years before it hit the atmosphere, mineral time capsules reveal
item.description: Why is there life on Earth? It's one of the oldest questions humans have asked, and as far as we know, our planet is the only one that holds the answer. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Astronauts to Answer Questions from Florida Students
item.description: Students in Florida will hear from NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney as they answer prerecorded STEM questions while aboard the International Space Station. The Earth-to-space call will begin at 12 p.m. EDT Friday, Oct. 16, and will stream live on the agency’s Learn With NASA YouTube channel. This event is hosted by Sally Ride Elementary School […] Fuente: NASA.

item.description: Journey beneath the waves and meet some of the residents that make the Great Barrier Reef such a biodiverse ecosystem. ... Ver más Tenemos problemas para reproducir este vídeo. Más información Fuente: National Geographic.

item.title: How can AI transform education without leaving anyone behind?
item.description: As artificial intelligence (AI) rapidly enters classrooms and learning environments, how can societies ensure that its benefits reach learners and educators while avoiding new forms of inequality? A new international study led by Associate Professor Rwitajit Majumdar at Kumamoto University in Japan provides a roadmap for responsible AI integration in education. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Museum specimens reveal pathogen behind decades-old mystery of disappearing frogs
item.description: In the 1970s, researchers began to observe drastic amphibian declines in Brazil's Atlantic Forest, a global hotspot of frog biodiversity. For decades, these disappearances remained a mystery. Now, new research from scientists at the Center for Conservation Genomics at the Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute (NZCBI) and Pennsylvania State University (PSU), published today in the journal Molecular Ecology, points to amphibian chytridiomycosis, a devastating infectious disease, as the likely culprit. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Border-hopping virus identified in Chilean pepper and tomato crops
item.description: An international team of scientists recently collaborated to identify a mysterious viral disease damaging pepper and tomato crops in Chile. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Most marine protected areas fail to curb fishing: Study
item.description: Fishing is increasing in most marine reserves worldwide in spite of conservation pledges, a study published Wednesday found. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Muscle cells self-organize into spirals, advancing efforts to engineer tiny blood vessels that regulate flow
item.description: Different tissues need different amounts of blood depending on what they are doing. Meeting those changing demands requires the circulatory system to continually balance how much blood flows to different regions of the body. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Indonesia rescues starved orangutan from fires: Officials
item.description: A female orangutan that was likely starving was evacuated Wednesday from an area razed by fire on the Indonesian island of Borneo, officials said, as the country rescues hundreds of animals affected by the blazes. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Storm Harry: Drifting buoys help improve early forecasts of extreme events in the Mediterranean Sea
item.description: A network of drifting buoys equipped with barometers can help improve weather forecasts of extreme Mediterranean storms by providing crucial atmospheric observations from areas of the sea where measurements are scarce. A new study published in the Quarterly Journal of the Royal Meteorological Society provides the first assessment of the impact of these observations during Storm Harry, which affected the Mediterranean region in January 2026. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Software advance brings complex quantum simulations to standard computers
item.description: A major software advance could aid the creation of bigger, more reliable quantum computers, a study suggests. Researchers have developed an algorithm that enables off-the-shelf computers to run quantum simulations previously only possible using the world's most powerful supercomputers. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Fighting off microbial invasions drains plants' iron stores, but one protein helps restore balance
item.description: Energy production in our cells, oxygen traveling in our blood and immune cells fighting infection all depend on iron, an essential mineral that enters the food chain when plants absorb it from soil. But iron is often scarce—likely increasingly so as global weather and temperatures continue to change—and we aren't the only ones that need it. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Bering Land Bridge base camp reveals what life was like nearly 14,000 years ago
item.description: The area of water between Russia and North America and the Pacific and Arctic oceans is now known as the Bering Strait. Yet it was once what we call the Bering Land Bridge, an exposed land and maritime region that connected Asia to North America. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Main factors in pornography use among adolescents identified
item.description: A study by the Universitat Rovira i Virgili (URV) has analyzed which factors are most associated with pornography use during adolescence. The results show that the most predictive variable is gender, followed by problematic internet use, cannabis and alcohol consumption, family conflict and engaging in certain risky sexual behaviors. The research, published in the journal Computation, was based on the 2023 ESTUDES survey and used a sample of 33,543 adolescents. The aim was to determine which personal, family, digital and behavioral variables are most useful for predicting whether an… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New DNA tool could help detect harmful algal blooms before they spread
item.description: A new study by researchers at the University of South Florida and Florida Atlantic University has demonstrated that a DNA sequencing tool can rapidly identify harmful algae in coastal waters, offering a new approach for monitoring species that could lead to improved methods for detecting potentially dangerous species before blooms become widespread. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Removing rats and restoring native plants could help atolls withstand rising seas
item.description: Protecting seabirds and restoring natural vegetation could give low-lying tropical atoll islands a fighting chance against the threat of sea-level rise, a new study reveals. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Warmer coastal waters drive heavy cyclone rainfall farther inland, raising flood risks
item.description: A research team at The Hong Kong Polytechnic University (PolyU) has found that the area affected by tropical cyclone (TC) rainfall is extending inland along Northern Hemisphere coasts at an average rate of approximately 3.8 kilometers (2.4 miles) per decade. Driven by rising nearshore sea surface temperature (SST), this shift is increasing disaster risks for inland regions. The work is published in the journal Nature Communications. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Nine studies reveal consumers favor eco-friendly additions over waste-cutting removals
item.description: When hotels replace single-use toiletries with refillable dispensers, or companies strip unnecessary items from product bundles to cut waste, they may expect consumers to hail these changes as environmentally responsible. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 'Sundown towns' linked to lingering racial bias
item.description: A sundown town is a community that prohibited Black people from staying within its borders after dark or from owning property. This was done through laws, signs, threats, harassment or violence. More than 150 years after the end of slavery and a generation after Civil Rights reforms, a new study finds that places designated as "sundown towns" in the past are more racist today. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Researchers use AI to design proteins that cut up other proteins
item.description: AI design tools make proteins that break bonds that are stable for hundreds of years. Fuente: Ars Technica.
item.dc:creator: John Timmer

item.title: Toothless 'hell chicken' dinosaur may have had a taste for fruit
item.description: While many dinosaurs were fearsome predators with razor-sharp teeth, others were peaceful herbivores munching on plants. We can now add a new species to the list of plant-eaters, Infernogallus jamesi. Its name means hell chicken, and its fossilized remains were found in the Hell Creek Formation, a fossil-rich rock formation extending across parts of Montana, South Dakota and North Dakota. And it is providing fresh insights into how some dinosaur diets evolved. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Local DNA motion inside the cell stays nearly constant throughout interphase
item.description: Human genomic DNA is wrapped around core histone proteins to form nucleosomes, the fundamental units of chromatin. During interphase, the period between cell divisions, DNA is replicated and the nucleus becomes larger. At the same time, cells must continuously carry out essential genome functions such as transcription, DNA replication and DNA repair. How the behavior of genomic DNA is maintained during these large changes has remained unclear. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA’s Chandra Breaks Down ‘Treble Clef’s’ Galaxy Cluster Collision
item.description: Astronomers have used NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory to break down the cause of a remarkable formation of radio waves they have nicknamed the “Treble Clef” because its distinct shape strongly resembles the musical symbol. The researchers discovered the Treble Clef is likely caused by an outburst from a supermassive black hole, followed by a collision […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Australia's oldest underwater archaeology reveals ancient life within a lost landscape
item.description: New discoveries from Australia's oldest known underwater archaeological record reveal how First Peoples lived, transported goods and used different places within a vast cultural landscape that was submerged when rising seas transformed the continent after the last ice age. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A tiny magnetic whirlpool could point to a new kind of ultra-efficient memory
item.description: Every time a computer stores or erases information, it uses energy. The amount is tiny for a single operation, but those operations happen billions of times every second. For decades, scientists have wondered just how little energy a memory device could use before reaching the fundamental theoretical limit set by the laws of physics. Now, researchers have shown that it is possible to come close. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 🧼 FUGA DE PELÍCULA: LOS ATRAPARON EN BOLIVIA Walter Ernesto Medina, de 29 años y nacionalidad dominicana, y Jaime Olmos Delgadillo, de 36 y nacionalidad boliviana, protagonizaron una fuga insólita en La Quiaca. Ambos estaban detenidos en una dependencia de Gendarmería Nacional y habrían utilizado detergente o jabón líquido para deslizarse entre las rejas y escapar. Por el momento, las autoridades no confirmaron qué sustancia usaron. La fuga activó un operativo de búsqueda y los dos hombres lograron cruzar hacia Bolivia. Sin embargo, las autoridades bolivianas los localizaron y los entregaron nuevamente a la Argentina a través del puente internacional que une Villazón con La Quiaca. La secuencia quedó registrada por cámaras de seguridad. Los dos detenidos volvieron a quedar bajo custodia argentina y deberán continuar con sus procesos judiciales. Ahora, los investigadores buscan establecer cómo lograron escapar y qué fallas de seguridad les permitieron abandonar el lugar sin que los efectivos advirtieran la maniobra a tiempo. ▶️Seguí el minuto a minuto de todas las noticias en nuestro canal de YouTube. #LaQuiaca #Fuga #Policiales #Insolito | Crónica TV

item.title: Satellites accurately detect methane emissions in largest controlled test yet
item.description: Researchers have conducted the largest-ever controlled test of space-based methane monitoring, finding that dedicated methane sensors correctly detected nearly all methane plumes released on clear days. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The stubby legs of ancient sled dogs helped people traverse the Arctic for the past 9,000 years
item.description: For centuries, dogs have helped people travel across the Arctic, hauling supplies, equipment and other goods through snowy landscapes where other domesticated animals struggled to venture. Now, a new study publishing Oct. 14 in the journal iScience finds that sled dogs might have evolved shorter legs that helped them pull loads more efficiently. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Sustained pressure halts cancer cell migration and triggers death in 3D lab models
item.description: The growth and death of cancer cells in the lab are studied primarily in two-dimensional cell cultures. In a study published in the journal Developmental Cell on Oct. 14, researchers instead used three-dimensional models to uncover how pressure and mechanical confinement impact cell growth—halting the cells' metastatic behavior and ultimately leading to their death. The findings could lead to the development of new biomarkers to predict which cancers are more likely to spread, or metastasize, and could ultimately lead to new approaches for preventing metastasis. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Robotic 'time crystal' organizes itself into a single rhythm despite random disturbances
item.description: Scientists have developed a material that can grow and coordinate its own movement until the entire structure pulses in unison, paving the way for versatile robots that behave more like living systems. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Microplastics are chemically active and could cause biological harm
item.description: Plastics are supposed to be chemically inert. It's the reason they're used so frequently to package food, bottle water and create children's toys: They're safe. But something important happens when a large piece of plastic fragments into micro- and nanoparticles. Its surface area increases dramatically relative to its volume. Vastly more of the material is now exposed to its surroundings. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Not all early birds evolved toward better flight, Jurassic fossil suggests
item.description: For early birds, evolution wasn't always about becoming better flyers. This conclusion is supported by the recent discovery of a remarkably well-preserved, 150-million-year-old bird fossil from Fujian province, China, which is challenging long-held assumptions about early bird evolution. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Modeling study shows early tetrapods had surprisingly little ability to move their necks
item.description: A new model using sturgeon as a material analog has made it possible to estimate how the backbones of some of the first animals on land could and could not move. These results disprove a long-standing hypothesis that changes in early tetrapod anatomy as they moved onto land gave them improved neck mobility. The study, led by a researcher at Uppsala University, formerly of Carleton University in Canada, has been published in the journal Nature. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI-enhanced weather model doubles predictive power two to six weeks out
item.description: In 2021, Texas suffered the worst energy infrastructure failure in state history, following three severe winter storms in February. At least 246 people were killed as a result of the disruptions, which led to food, water, heat and electricity shortages. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Little fish, big deal—Record haul of baby sturgeons offers hope for the future
item.description: Just a few centimeters long, slimy and covered in razor-sharp spines, baby sturgeons look like creatures from one of the Alien movies. But for the people who pull them from the river, these diminutive ugly ducklings of the fish world are a beautiful sight. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Develops Batteries to Power Humanity’s Return to Moon
item.description: If you’ve ever had your car start sluggishly, or not at all, on a particularly frigid winter morning, you know standard batteries do not like extreme cold. That’s why NASA researchers are working to develop a battery that could function in the brutal cold of the Moon’s South Pole, where nighttime temperatures plunge to minus […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Joseph Atkinson

item.title: Team builds resource-sharing technology platform for nonprofits
item.description: Nonprofit organizations have historically struggled with underfunding, scarce resources and even identifying what physical, human, social and financial capital they already have. But what if there were an easy way they could share surplus assets with other social enterprises to make better use of their collective resources and increase their community impact? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Could a molecular ZIP code unlock treatments for untreatable diseases?
item.description: Imagine a medicine that stops seizures at their source, switches off instructions that keep a cancerous tumor growing and prevents Alzheimer's from stealing memories and wreaking havoc on the brain. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Bending Spoons skyrockets 35% as Berkshire Hathaway makes $330 million investment
item.description: Berkshire's latest investment follows the $600 million it invested in the company's IPO this July. Fuente: CNBC - World.

item.title: How shark ecotourism sparks long-term conservation
item.description: People who join shark ecotourism tours are more likely to take action to protect sharks, including donating to related causes, signing petitions or speaking up online, new research from the University of Sydney shows. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: DNA analysis uncovers first known genetic connection between rare New Caledonian plant and parasitic plant
item.description: A new genetic analysis tool developed by UF assistant professor of biology Liming Cai, Ph.D., has led to the discovery of the first known interaction between Amborella, a rare New Caledonian plant, and a parasitic plant called Hachettea. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Your dog may link sounds with shapes, just like you do
item.description: Sounds have shapes. That might sound strange since sound waves are invisible, but a famous psychological experiment in the 1920s showed that our brains naturally link spoken sounds to visual forms. According to new research published in Proceedings of the Royal Society B, dogs may do this too. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Jamming the flow to enable memory in quantum materials
item.description: Understanding and controlling phase transitions are fundamental to physics and central to many technological revolutions. There is currently strong interest in materials with coupled structural and electronic phase transitions, where controlling the transition plasticity naturally yields built-in memory—a key step in emulating neurons and synapses for "neuromorphic" or brain-like computing technologies. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Chemists develop blueprint for designing powerful fluorescent materials for better disease detection
item.description: The team, led by professors Simon Lewis and Tony James and Dr. Dan Pantos in the university's Department of Chemistry, has transformed azulene, a naturally occurring blue compound found in certain mushrooms and corals, into a versatile tool for biological imaging and chemical sensing. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Consumer prices rose 3.7% annually in September as gas prices skyrocket
item.description: The consumer price index was expected to increase 0.6% in September on a monthly basis and 3.6% from a year ago, according to the Dow Jones consensus forecast. Fuente: CNBC - World.

item.title: New evidence points to two feeding black holes just 175 parsecs apart lurking in the early universe
item.description: Astronomers have found two actively feeding supermassive black holes separated by just 175 parsecs (570 light-years) in a galaxy seen when the universe was only about 2 billion years old. The system, MG B2016+112, lies at a redshift of 3.273 and is the most compact dual AGN known at this redshift. The study was posted to the arXiv preprint server on Sept. 25. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How lessons from fisheries management could help us govern Earth's orbital space
item.description: The space industry is rapidly expanding. About 20,000 satellites already circle Earth, a number that could reach 100,000 by 2030. They bring growing environmental costs: space debris, collision risks, atmospheric pollution from launches and reentry and interference with astronomical observations. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA to Discuss Artemis Acceleration, Status of Upcoming Moon Missions
item.description: NASA will provide an update on its plans to return American astronauts to the surface of the Moon by 2028 at 2 p.m. EDT, Friday, Oct. 23, at the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Learn where to watch online: https://www.nasa.gov/live Participants in the briefing include: The update will include details about NASA’s Artemis III […] Fuente: NASA.
